title: The great board game comeback
intro: A magazine-style article about why so many people are going back to playing games around a table. Ola is a made-up café owner, not a real person; the article was written for Psotek English
paras: Ten years ago, many people thought board games were finished. Why would anyone roll dice and move little pieces around a piece of cardboard when they could play exciting games on a phone? Yet today, board games are enjoying a surprising comeback. Specialist shops are opening in many cities, and in some cafés you have to book a table days in advance.

Ola, who runs a small board game café in Wrocław, says her customers are mostly young adults. "Many of them spend all day in front of screens at work," she explains. "In the evening, they want something they can touch." Her café has more than four hundred games on its shelves, from quick card games that take ten minutes to huge adventures that can last a whole afternoon.

One reason for the comeback is that modern games are very different from the ones our grandparents played. Instead of simply throwing dice and hoping for luck, players often have to plan, trade and make difficult decisions. Some games are cooperative: everyone plays together against the game itself, so nobody goes home as the loser. This makes them popular with families and with people who do not enjoy competition. Some even tell a story that changes every time you play, so no two evenings are the same.

Another reason is social. When you play online, your opponent may be on the other side of the world. Around a table, you see people's faces, hear their jokes and notice when someone is bluffing. Many players say that this kind of face-to-face contact makes them feel closer to their friends, especially at a time when so much of life happens through a screen.

Of course, board games are not always peaceful. Arguments about the rules are common, and some families have a famous game that nobody is allowed to suggest any more because it always ends in tears. But for many players, that is part of the fun. As Ola puts it, "A screen can show you a game. A table gives you an evening."

levels.title: Tomek and his red bike
levels.intro: A short, easy text about a boy and his bike. Tomek and his family are made-up people; the text was written for Psotek English
paras: This is Tomek. He is eleven years old, and he lives in Gdańsk with his mum, his dad and his little sister, Zosia. Tomek has a red bike. He loves it very much.
Every morning, Tomek rides his bike to school. The school is two kilometres from his house. He always wears a helmet, and he stops at every red light. The ride takes fifteen minutes.
On Saturdays, Tomek and his dad ride to the beach. They take sandwiches and water. Zosia is only five, so she sits in a small seat on Dad's bike. She sings songs all the way!
Last week, Tomek's bike had a flat tyre. His dad showed him how to fix it. Now Tomek can fix his bike on his own, and he is very proud.

levels.title: The night the lights went out
levels.intro: A short story about a family evening without electricity. Marta and her family are made-up people; the text was written for Psotek English
paras: My name is Marta. Last winter, on a cold Tuesday evening, all the lights in our flat suddenly went out. The fridge stopped humming, the TV went black and my brother's computer game disappeared in the middle of a battle. We looked out of the window. The whole street was dark.

At first, everybody was annoyed. My dad wanted to watch the football, and I had homework to finish. Then my mum found some candles in a kitchen drawer and lit them on the table. Our living room looked warm and golden, like a picture in an old book.

We couldn't cook dinner because our cooker is electric, so we ate bread, cheese and apples. After that, my dad taught us a card game from his childhood. He won the first three games, but then my little brother won five games in a row and laughed so much that he fell off his chair.

Later, my grandmother phoned us. Her lights were off too, so she told us stories about her village when she was young. In her village, there was no electricity in the evenings, and people sang songs together after dinner.
The lights came back at half past ten. Everyone was a little sad. Now, once a month, we have a 'dark evening': no screens, just candles, cards and stories.

levels.title: Why we forget names (and how to stop)
levels.intro: An article about one of the most common memory problems and a few simple tricks that help. It was written for Psotek English
paras: You are introduced to someone at a party. You shake hands, smile, hear their name clearly, and ten seconds later it has vanished without a trace. If this sounds familiar, you are in good company. Forgetting names is one of the most common memory complaints, and it happens to people who can remember phone numbers, song lyrics and the plots of entire TV series without breaking a sweat.

Part of the problem is that names are surprisingly arbitrary. If someone tells you they are a baker, the word connects to a whole network of things you already know: bread, early mornings, the smell of a warm kitchen. A surname like Baker, on the other hand, tells you nothing about the person standing in front of you. Your brain files the job under dozens of familiar labels, while the name gets filed under nothing at all. With nothing to hook onto, it simply slips away.

Attention plays a role too. When we meet someone new, our minds are usually busy elsewhere. We are thinking about how we look, what we are going to say next, or whether there is spinach in our teeth. The name is spoken, but it never really gets through the door, so strictly speaking we have not forgotten it at all. We never learned it in the first place. Nerves make this worse, which is why names are so often lost at job interviews and on first dates, exactly the moments when we most want to get them right.

Fortunately, a few simple tricks can make names stick. The first is to use the name straight away: "Nice to meet you, Agata." Saying it aloud gives your brain a second chance to store it. The second is to link the name to something vivid, such as picturing a Mr Fox with a bushy orange tail. The sillier the picture, the better it tends to work. Finally, try writing names down after an event, especially if you are likely to meet the same people again.

None of these methods is magic, and everyone has the occasional blank moment. If it happens, honesty is usually the best policy. Most people are far less offended than we imagine, especially if you admit it with a smile. After all, there is a good chance they have forgotten yours too.

levels.title: In praise of the handwritten note
levels.intro: An opinion piece on why writing by hand may still be worth the effort in a world of keyboards. It was written for Psotek English
paras: It would be easy to dismiss handwriting as a charming relic, something to be filed alongside fax machines and printed maps. Most of us type far more than we write; many of us struggle to read our own shopping lists. And yet there are reasons to think that abandoning the pen entirely might cost us more than we realise.

The first concerns learning. A number of studies have suggested that students who take notes by hand tend to remember the material better than those who type, perhaps because writing is too slow to allow word-for-word transcription. Forced to choose what matters, the hand-writer has to process ideas rather than merely record them. The evidence is not conclusive, and the effect may well depend on the task, but it is at least plausible that a little friction is good for the mind. Writing also seems to engage the hands and eyes in a way that tapping keys does not, although researchers continue to argue about how much this matters.

The second reason is more personal. A typed message, however warm, arrives in the same font as a gas bill. A handwritten note carries traces of the person who wrote it: the slant of the letters, a crossed-out word, the pressure of the pen when they were in a hurry. It is, in a modest way, a physical piece of someone's time. It is hardly surprising, then, that people keep birthday cards for decades while deleting thousands of emails without a second thought. Letters from grandparents, recipes in a parent's hand, a note slipped into a lunchbox: these are objects that people carry from one home to the next for a lifetime.

None of this is to suggest that we should turn back the clock. Keyboards are faster, more legible and far more accessible for people with certain disabilities; insisting on handwriting in every context would be both impractical and unfair. Speed and clarity matter, and they are not to be dismissed lightly. Nor is there anything inherently virtuous about a fountain pen. A thoughtless message does not become profound simply because it is written in ink.

What I would argue for is a deliberate, occasional return. A thank-you note after a dinner, a few lines on a postcard, the outline of a talk scribbled on paper rather than a screen: small acts like these cost little and may give back a surprising amount. Handwriting need not compete with technology. It simply offers something that technology, for all its convenience, has never quite managed to replicate. Even a single handwritten paragraph a week might be enough to keep the habit, and the hand, from disappearing altogether.

levels.title: On getting lost
levels.intro: A reflective essay on the forgotten pleasures of losing your way in a city. It was written for Psotek English
paras: There is a particular species of pleasure available only to those who have mislaid their bearings. It arrives, typically, a few minutes after the initial panic: the map app has lost its signal, the street names have stopped making sense, and you are forced, against every modern instinct, simply to look. The city, which a moment ago was a sequence of instructions, becomes a place again. Shop signs, the angle of the light, the sound of a tram two streets away: all of it suddenly matters.

We have grown remarkably efficient at not getting lost. The blue dot on the screen tells us where we are with uncanny precision, and the route it proposes is almost always the shortest. The app knows the fastest way to the museum; it has no opinion on whether the museum is the best thing we will see that day. Yet efficiency has a way of flattening experience. When we follow the line, we arrive; we rarely wander. The side street with the bakery that smells of cardamom, the courtyard glimpsed through a half-open gate, the square where old men argue over chess: these are, by definition, not on the way to anywhere.

Writers have long celebrated the art of aimless walking. The nineteenth-century flâneur drifted through Paris with no purpose beyond observation, and countless essayists since have insisted that a city reveals itself only to those who are in no hurry. Strolling becomes a form of reading, and the pavement a text whose margins are as interesting as its headlines. One need not romanticise this too much, since getting lost in the rain with a dying phone and a train to catch is rarely poetic, but the underlying insight holds water. Attention, not distance, is what turns a journey into an experience.

There is also, I suspect, a subtler benefit. Being lost is a small, safe rehearsal for uncertainty. It asks us to tolerate not knowing, to read clues, to ask a stranger for help and to accept that the answer may come in a language we only half understand. In a culture that prizes control and treats every delay as a failure, an hour of disorientation can be oddly restorative, a reminder that the world is larger and less predictable than our itineraries suggest. Small mistakes are survivable, and survivable mistakes are where confidence is quietly built.

None of this requires abandoning technology wholesale. It requires only the occasional decision to leave the phone in a pocket and take the turning that looks interesting rather than the one that looks correct. The worst that can happen, in most places, is that we arrive a little late. The best is that we stumble upon something no algorithm would have thought to recommend, and perhaps rediscover the half-forgotten art of finding our own way.
